title: Build Cool Tools Fast
outcome: Find a problem worth solving, build a tool that solves it, get real users, and make it sustainable — repeatedly, using AI to move fast without shipping garbage.

phases.name: Ideas & Planning
phases.outcome: Generate, filter and validate tool ideas so you build things people actually use, scoped to what you can actually ship.

modules.name: Where Ideas Actually Come From
modules.objective: Generate tool ideas from observed friction rather than from brainstorming.
lessons: Your own annoyance is the best signal you have
Watching how people work around a missing tool
The spreadsheet that's secretly an application
Ideas from communities you're already in
Keeping an idea log that's worth rereading
practice: Turn eight observed frictions into tool ideas
lab: Log two weeks of friction
An idea log with at least fifteen entries and three candidates marked

modules.name: Finding Out Before You Build
modules.objective: Test whether an idea is wanted before spending weeks on it.
lessons: Nobody will tell you your idea is bad, so ask differently
Asking about behaviour, not about intentions
The existing solution people already put up with
Cheap signals: a landing page, a post, a waitlist
Killing an idea early and cheaply
practice: Design a validation test for seven ideas
lab: Validate one idea before writing code
A validation record with what you asked, who answered, and your go/no-go

modules.name: Cutting It Down to Shippable
modules.objective: Reduce an idea to the smallest version that's genuinely useful.
lessons: The version that's useful in one week
Features to cut, and the one you can't
Manual behind the curtain: faking the hard part
Scoping to a week you might spend in bed
practice: Cut seven bloated specs to a week's work
lab: Scope your tool to a one-week build
A scoped spec with an explicit cut list and the one job it does

modules.name: Who It's For
modules.objective: Define a specific user well enough that design decisions become obvious.
lessons: Designing for the person with no energy today
practice: Sharpen seven vague audience definitions
lab: Write the user definition for your tool
A user definition specific enough to settle three real design arguments

modules.name: What Already Exists
modules.objective: Find what's already out there and decide honestly whether to build anyway.

Why an existing tool isn't good enough, specifically
Free, open source, and competing with those
Building it anyway for a good reason
Building it anyway for a bad reason
practice: Assess seven ideas against what exists
lab: Do the competitive research on your idea
A written assessment of five existing tools and your specific differentiation

phases.name: CLI Tools
phases.outcome: Build command-line tools people can install, script around, and depend on — beyond the first working version.

modules.name: Designing a CLI People Won't Fight
modules.objective: Design a command-line interface with sensible defaults, discoverable flags and predictable behaviour.
lessons: Commands and subcommands: shaping the mental model
Flags, arguments and defaults that need no manual
Output that works in a pipe and for a human
Interactive prompts versus flags: when each is right
practice: Redesign seven confusing CLI interfaces
lab: Design the interface for a new CLI before writing code
A written interface spec with help text and three example invocations

modules.name: State, Config and Secrets
modules.objective: Manage a CLI tool's configuration and credentials without embarrassing yourself.
lessons: Where a CLI tool should keep its state
Config files: format, location, and sane precedence
Environment variables and when to prefer them
Storing a credential without writing it in plaintext everywhere
Migrating a config format without breaking existing users
practice: Fix seven config-handling mistakes
lab: Add persistent config to your CLI tool
A tool that reads and writes config safely, with a credential stored properly

modules.name: Errors, Exit Codes and Scriptability
modules.objective: Make a CLI tool safe to script around by other programs, not just run by hand.
lessons: Exit codes are an API, not an afterthought
Error messages aimed at the person who'll actually read them
Machine-readable output as an explicit mode
Failing loudly instead of silently continuing
Testing a CLI tool the way a script would call it
practice: Fix seven scripts that break other scripts
lab: Make your CLI tool safe to pipe and script
A tool with correct exit codes, a --json mode, and a test that scripts against it

modules.name: Packaging and Distribution
modules.objective: Get a CLI tool onto someone else's machine with one command.
lessons: What "install this" actually requires of a stranger
Publishing to npm properly: versioning and the files that ship
Cross-platform gotchas: paths, shells, line endings
Auto-update, and why most tools shouldn't have it
Writing an install section nobody gets stuck on
practice: Fix seven broken install instructions
lab: Publish your CLI tool for real
A published package a stranger installed and ran from your README alone

modules.name: Putting AI Inside a CLI Tool
modules.objective: Use an AI step inside a command-line tool without making it slow, expensive or flaky.
lessons: Where an AI call belongs in a fast local tool
Streaming output so the terminal doesn't feel frozen

Falling back when the API is unavailable
Keeping an AI-powered CLI tool's cost predictable
practice: Design the AI step and fallback for seven CLI ideas
lab: Add an AI-powered command to a CLI tool

phases.name: Web Applications
phases.outcome: Build and ship web apps that hold up past the first demo — real state, real deployment, real AI integration.

modules.name: Structuring a Web App That Grows

Routing for a tool with more than one screen

modules.name: Deploying and Managing Environments

modules.name: Errors and Loading States People Trust
modules.objective: Handle every state a screen can be in, not just the happy path.

phases.name: Monetization & Scaling
phases.outcome: Turn a working tool into an API worth paying for, price it defensibly, and keep it running as usage grows.

Error responses that are actually useful
Pagination that doesn't fall over at scale
Documentation that is also the contract
practice: Fix seven poorly-designed API endpoints
lab: Design and document a real API for your tool

phases.name: Testing & Debugging

Deciding what actually needs a test here
